query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A multiscale simulation approach that integrates defect‐aware DFT potentials with atomistic models for phonon and electron scattering will yield independent and quantitatively accurate predictions for the lattice and electronic thermal conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr. This method is expected to reduce prediction errors by at least 20–30% compared to traditional Debye‐temperature-based analytical models.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, considered both as an idealized defect‐free bulk crystal and as a material with realistic impurity levels (e.g., ~1 wt.% oxygen) that introduce local disorder.
generation.intervention: Application of a defect-aware multiscale simulation that couples first-principles DFT (capturing atomic-scale defect/disorder effects) with explicit atomistic modeling of phonon and electronic scattering to compute lattice and electronic heat transport separately.
generation.conditions: The approach is applicable across a wide temperature range, specifically at low temperatures (<200 K) where lattice and electronic contributions are expected to be comparable, and at high temperatures (300–1200 K) where experimental total conductivities fall between 10 and 17 W/(K·m).
generation.structural_mediator: Local disorder and variations in interatomic force constants induced by defects and impurities (e.g., oxygen incorporation) that affect phonon and electron scattering mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: By explicitly accounting for defect-induced local variations using defect-aware DFT and by distinguishing between phonon (lattice) and electron scattering processes, the model avoids the oversimplifications of Debye-temperature-based methods and unified analytical estimates. This separation allows for a more accurate reproduction of the underlying physics governing thermal transport in both pristine and impurity-bearing samples.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict separate lattice and electronic contributions that sum to a total thermal conductivity in agreement with experimental findings: similar magnitudes (within ±25% agreement) for both contributions at temperatures below 200 K, and a total conductivity within the experimental 10–17 W/(K·m) window at high temperatures. Overall, a reduction in predictive error by at least 20–30% relative to earlier approaches is expected.
generation.baseline: Previous approaches based on variations in atomic mass, force constants, Debye approximations, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled with analytical estimates that assume perfect, defect-free crystals and conflate the lattice and electronic heat transport mechanisms.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr in its conventional alloyed and oxygen-doped forms over temperatures below 200 K (for separate channel comparisons) and between 300–1200 K for total conductivity. It may not directly extend to conditions outside these temperature ranges or to alloys with impurity levels significantly different from ~1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement (20–30% reduction in error) depends on the accuracy with which defect and disorder effects are captured and on the precision of separating electron and phonon scattering processes. Variability in sample preparation and measurement techniques may also affect the comparison.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize high-purity HfNbTaTiZr samples with and without ~1 wt.% oxygen doping. Use temperature-dependent thermal conductivity measurements to independently isolate lattice and electronic contributions at low temperatures (<200 K) (through techniques such as applying external fields or other separation methods) and to measure total conductivity at high temperatures (300–1200 K). Compare these experimental measurements with the predictions from the new multiscale simulation approach.
measurements: Total thermal conductivity in the 300–1200 K range
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the model’s predicted separate contributions differ by more than ±25% from the corresponding experimental values at low temperatures, or if the high-temperature total conductivity prediction falls outside the 10–17 W/(K·m) range, or if the overall error reduction is less than 20% compared to traditional Debye-based models, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . frame.system: Refractory high‐entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr, originally considered as a defect‐free bulk crystal but with experimental specimens that may include impurities (e.g., 1 wt.% oxygen) and associated local disorder.
frame.goal: Develop a predictive model that independently and accurately resolves the lattice (phonon) and electronic contributions to thermal conductivity, without conflating them, across a broad temperature range.
frame.limitation: Existing analytical and simulation approaches either rely on simplified, perfect-crystal assumptions (ignoring defects and full atomic-scale complexity) or require external parameters (e.g., Debye temperature) that prevent a clear separation of lattice and electronic transport mechanisms.

frame.regime: The approach should be valid across a broad temperature spectrum—from low temperatures (where electronic and phonon contributions are comparable, e.g. below 200 K) to high temperatures (300–1200 K) as demonstrated in experimental observations—with specific attention to impurity effects (e.g., 1 wt.% O).

Temperature-dependent lattice heat transport analyses relied on simplified Debye or analytical models

frame.testable_hypothesis: A new predictive approach based on multiscale simulation—integrating first-principles calculations for defect and disorder effects with atomistic modeling of phonon and electron scattering mechanisms—will yield separate, quantitatively accurate predictions for lattice and electronic heat transport. It is expected to outperform earlier methods by reducing the predictive error by at least 20–30% relative to current Debye-based models and unified conductivity estimates. The model should accurately predict the thermal conductivity spectra in defect-free samples as well as in specimens with realistic impurity levels (e.g., 1 wt.% oxygen) over the full measured temperature range. Decisive falsification could occur if, at low temperatures (<200 K), the predicted comparable contributions of lattice and electron conduction differ by more than ±25% from refined experimental measurements, or if high-temperature (300–1200 K) total conductivity predictions fall outside the 10–17 W/(K·m) range reported by experiments.
